sections.html:
Every parcel is assessed once a year as of July 1 at sixty percent of its true and actual value. A county levy rate applies the following calendar year, and the county sheriff then mails the bill and collects it in halves. W. Va. Code 11-3-1 sets the assessment date as July 1 of the year before the tax year, with the tax year being the next calendar year that begins after that date.

For a seller the calendar is the useful part. The July 1 value drives next year's bill, the bill goes out in summer, and the first half is due early in September. If you close partway through the cycle, seller and buyer have to split the bill between them.

  • Assessor: sets values for real and personal property and keeps the records.
  • County commission: acts as the board of equalization and review every February.
  • Levying bodies: the state, county commission, school board and any municipality set rates, within limits.
  • Sheriff: sends the tax ticket and collects payment.

That phrase means the price the property would bring if the owner offered it voluntarily on the usual terms, not a forced-sale price (W. Va. Code 11-3-1(a)). For owner-occupied homes, the assessor also weighs the fair and reasonable income the property might earn as a rental under normal local conditions.

Assessors keep values current by sending a staff member to each parcel of real property in repeating three-year cycles to check for changes. The sixty percent rule is firm: assessed value must be 60 percent of true and actual value, and the tax is the levy rate applied to the assessed figure.

West Virginia sorts property into four classes, and the class caps the rate.

  • Class I: tangible personal property used exclusively in agriculture, farm products held by the producer, and intangible personal property.
  • Class II: homes the owner lives in and uses only as a residence, plus farms occupied and cultivated by their owners or bona fide tenants.
  • Class III: every other kind of real and personal property outside city limits.
  • Class IV: every other kind of real and personal property inside city limits.

Figures are ceilings on regular levies, stated in cents per $100 of assessed value. Voters in a county, school district or municipality can approve excess levies above them, but the state itself can't exceed its rate. Statewide, the average rate across all property is $1.90 per $100 of assessed valuation. Your own rate depends on your levy district and any excess levies, so read the sheriff's ticket for the real number.

You pay in two halves (W. Va. Code 11A-1-3(a)). Half one falls due September 1 of the tax year and turns delinquent on October 1. Half two falls due March 1 and turns delinquent on April 1.

  • Assessment date: the July 1 before the tax year begins.
  • Tax tickets from sheriffs: on or after July 15 of the tax year.
  • Public utility bills from the State Auditor: June of the tax year.
  • Discount for paying by the due date: 2.5 percent.
  • Interest on delinquent taxes: 9 percent per year.

Pay on or before the payable date and you take the two and one-half percent discount. Miss it and interest at nine percent per annum runs from the delinquency date until the tax is paid. Each ticket goes to the last known address by first-class mail, yet section 11A-1-8 preserves the right to collect the tax, interest or penalty even if the sheriff fails to send the ticket or the taxpayer fails to get it. After buying or selling a house, make sure the ticket is going to the right address.

It exists for older and disabled owners. Under W. Va. Code 11-6B-3, the first $20,000 of assessed value is exempt on a homestead that the owner lives in and uses only as a home, provided the owner is 65 or older or certified permanently and totally disabled.

  • Two straight calendar years of West Virginia residence before the tax year are required, with narrow exceptions for people who left and came back and for certain military service members.
  • Collecting a comparable exemption in another state disqualifies you, and the application includes a sworn affidavit on the point.
  • One exemption per homestead, however many eligible owners share it.
  • The exemption attaches to the homestead occupied on the July 1 assessment date and applies to the next tax year.

A sale changes things. If a qualified owner's homestead passes by deed, will or any other way, the $20,000 comes off at the next July 1 assessment unless the new owner qualifies, so a buyer shouldn't count on the seller's lower bill. Under section 11-6B-4, an owner 65 or older who has filed once with the assessor needn't refile unless moving to a new homestead.

Talk to the assessor first. If that fails, go to the county commission, which sits as the board of equalization and review in February. Section 11-3-24 requires the commission to convene by February 1 of the tax year, lets it adjourn after February 15 and requires it to adjourn by the last day of February.

The board reviews and corrects valuation but can't decide questions of classification or taxability. For a classification dispute, section 11-3-24a lets a taxpayer ask the assessor for information and protest, with a path on to the Tax Commissioner and the Office of Tax Appeals. The board can bring any assessment found above or below sixty percent back to sixty percent, and no assessment can be raised without at least five days' written notice.

Skip the board meeting and you waive the right to seek correction of the current year's list, except by appeal to the Office of Tax Appeals or as otherwise provided. A taxpayer who elects a hearing may appeal the board's order to that office. Section 11-3-23a also provides an informal review: apply for relief to the board or the Office of Tax Appeals by February 20 of the tax year with a written protest.

The deadlines are tight and a missed February meeting can cost a year, so put them on your calendar early.

sections.h2: Taxes and fees when you sell
sections.html:
The deed carries the real property transfer tax of $1.10 per $500 of value or fraction, along with a $20 fee for transferring real estate for consideration (W. Va. Code 11-22-2). Both are collected by the county clerk at recording. That section also treats the excise tax as a county tax that the collecting county keeps, beginning July 1, 2025.

Recording happens at the county courthouse through the clerk, while the sheriff handles property tax. At closing, the title company or closing agent should pull a current tax statement from the sheriff, check which halves are paid, and settle any unpaid ones out of your proceeds.

Owe back taxes? Get a payoff figure from the county sheriff before you pick a buyer. A cash sale to us as-is can include a house with tax due, and we can walk through the numbers with you. The amount depends on the house and the payoff, and we promise no price.

faqs.q: What is the West Virginia property tax assessment ratio?
faqs.a: Sixty percent. Each year property is assessed as of July 1 at sixty percent of its true and actual value (W. Va. Code 11-3-1(a)), and the levy rate applies to that assessed figure.

faqs.q: When is the first half of West Virginia property tax due?
faqs.a: September 1 of the tax year, with delinquency starting October 1. Half two is due March 1 and delinquent April 1 (W. Va. Code 11A-1-3). Pay by the due dates to get a 2.5 percent discount.

faqs.q: What interest applies to late West Virginia property tax?
faqs.a: Nine percent a year, from the delinquency date until the tax is paid. It applies to both halves.

faqs.q: Who qualifies for the homestead exemption?
faqs.a: Owners who are 65 or older, or certified permanently and totally disabled, and who live in the house they own. The exemption removes the first $20,000 of assessed value and requires two straight calendar years of state residency, subject to the exceptions in section 11-6B-3.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house while property tax is still owed?
faqs.a: Yes. Closing normally pays the balance out of your proceeds. Ask the county sheriff for a payoff figure first, and be upfront with any buyer about what is owed.
